python3 app.py
# open http://localhost:8000

No pip install, no API keys, no accounts. Just Python's standard library and Ollama.

How I Built It

My process: from a text box to a meal planner

The idea came from my own fridge. My goal for this week was simply to learn and to submit, so I picked something small that I'd actually use. I built it with Claude as a coding partner, and the journey went like this.

1. Start simple. Version 1 was a text box and a button: ingredients in, recipes out. It worked, and it was boring.

2. Add layers, one real annoyance at a time. Every layer came from using it myself:

  • 🧂 Spices, because the model cheerfully called for saffron I don't own
  • 🥫 Cupboard, so it knows I have stock cubes and rice without asking
  • Meal, cuisine and kind of dish, so I can ask for a Mexican breakfast or a soup tonight
  • 📖 My recipes: save favourites, or import from the web (it reads the recipe card hidden in most recipe sites, and gemma3 cleans up pasted pages, skipping the life story and the adverts)
  • ❄️ Freezer portions: tonight's dinner becomes Wednesday's lunch
  • 🛒 On a budget, the idea from my first users: reduced "eat today" specials, with prices, within a budget

3. Make it think like a cook. The model would never say "you can nearly make your own asparagus soup". So the code matches the fridge against my saved recipes, and knows that a shallot will do for an onion and that stock in the cupboard counts. When I have 6 of 7 ingredients, my own recipe comes first. Then it looks at what the soup doesn't use (carrots, celery, half a lemon) and turns that into a side: soup and roasted veg chips, a winner for families, and more of the fridge used up.

4. Hit the wall: my laptop. Every layer made the prompt longer and the answer longer. I'm running a 4B model on a laptop with 7 GB of RAM and no GPU. I measured it: gemma3 reads about 25 tokens (word pieces) a second here, and writes about 10. By the time it was writing two recipes, each with a side, one answer took three minutes, longer when it had to ask again.

5. Design around the device. Instead of giving up features, I cut what each answer costs: a shorter prompt (the model only needs a saved recipe's ingredients, not its whole method), shorter steps, fewer retries, and one idea at a time with a 🔄 Another idea button. The first idea, my own soup with chips on the side, now arrives in about a minute.

6. Where it's going. I picture Fridge2Fork as a phone app you use in the supermarket aisle: you see the reduced specials, add them, see what you can make, and cook it at home that night. Small Gemma models already run on phones, so it could stay offline, private and free.

The closed tool helped me build it, and the open model is it.

How it works 

browser form ─► app.py ─► gemma3 (4B) via Ollama ─► JSON ─► recipe cards
 fridge, spices,  builds the   runs on my laptop's CPU    validated,
 cupboard, meal,  prompt                                  cleaned up
 cuisine, diet
  • app.py is a small Python server using only the standard library. It serves the page and has one endpoint, /api/recipes.
  • It builds a prompt from everything you chose and sends it to gemma3 (4B) running locally in Ollama, with format: "json" so the reply comes back as structured data: name, pitch, minutes, uses, also_need, steps.
  • It validates the reply and retries if the model returns broken or incomplete JSON.
  • index.html is a single page with no frameworks and no build step. It renders the recipe cards and remembers your cupboard in the browser.

On my laptop (7 GB of RAM, no GPU), the first idea takes about a minute (40 seconds without a side). The page shows a little bobbing 🍲 and a timer so you know it's working.

Things that went wrong (and what I learned)

"NetworkError when attempting to fetch resource." The first time I tried it, I double-clicked index.html instead of going to localhost:8000. A page opened from a file has no server behind it, so the request went nowhere. Now the page detects that and talks to the local server directly, and if the server isn't running, it tells you so in plain English.

The model listed things I already had. Early on, "You'd also need" kept saying olive oil and butter. Telling it plainly that oil, butter, flour, sugar and water are always available fixed most of that. But even with the cupboard list, it once told me I'd need rice when rice was ticked. Rather than keep arguing with the prompt, I filter those out in code. Lesson: a small model follows instructions mostly, so check the important rules in code.

I almost had the model ask questions. I wanted it to ask "do you have stock cubes?" before suggesting recipes. But on a CPU, every round trip costs about 40 seconds, so a back-and-forth would have been painful. A cupboard checklist gives the model the same information instantly. Lesson: with a local model, design around latency.

Restricting spices made the recipes better. Once the model could only use the spices I'd ticked, the recipes went from "nice idea, but I don't have saffron" to things I could actually cook tonight.

Every recipe was a hash, a stew, a bake or a scramble. Give a small model four vegetables and it plays it safe, every time. People would get bored by day three. So now the code picks the style, not the model: each request draws two different styles (stir-fry, curry, fritters, dumplings…) and gemma fills them in. If you ask for a soup, the app checks that both answers really are soups, and asks again if not. Lesson: a small model is a good writer but a poor decider, so make the decisions in code.

A risotto with no rice. The random styles once gave me a "cauliflower risotto" when I had no rice. A risotto without rice isn't a risotto. Now a style that's built on a base (rice, pasta, tortillas, bread, pastry, eggs) is only picked when that base is in your fridge or cupboard.

"Taco spice" meant tacos. I had taco spice ticked, and gemma kept slipping tortillas into everything, even a soup. Telling it "a spice is only seasoning" helped, but the real fix was code again: if a recipe leans on a base you don't have, the app asks once more.

Old recipes sneaking in. With just three ingredients, I'd get dishes using things I'd never typed. The app wasn't remembering past requests: my saved recipes were. Any saved recipe sharing a single word with my fridge ("chicken") went into the prompt with its whole ingredient list, and gemma used the lot. Now a saved recipe is only used automatically when you have at least 40% of it, and the others are shown as buttons so you choose.

Every feature made it slower. This was the biggest obstacle of the week. Each layer added words to the prompt and to the answer, and on a CPU every word costs time: from about 40 seconds to three minutes. Measuring it (about 25 tokens a second in, 10 out) showed exactly where the time went, and asking for one idea at a time got the first answer back to about a minute. Lesson: on a small device, the length of every prompt and reply is part of the design.

A shallot isn't an onion (to a computer). The app said I had only 1 of the 9 ingredients for my own asparagus soup. It didn't know shallots and onions are interchangeable, it counted butter and oil as missing, it ignored the stock in my cupboard, and it counted "bread to serve (optional)" against me. With simple swap rules, it now says 6 of 7.

What I'd add next

Fridge2Fork is a proof of concept: it shows that a 4B model on a 7 GB laptop can already plan dinner. From here, it can grow in two directions without giving up being open.

Version 1.5

  • 🍳 My kitchen: tick what you own (soup maker, blender, Thermomix, air fryer, slow cooker) and recipes are written for it: "add everything to the soup maker, smooth setting". And nobody gets told to blend who doesn't own a blender.
  • ⚖️ Quantities: amounts for each ingredient, scaled to servings and freezer portions in code, because scaling is maths, and maths is what small models get wrong.

Beyond that

  • Bigger open models. A 4B model has a small imagination. With leftover veg and a cauliflower, it never suggested the obvious veggie cottage pie (sauté the veg, mash the cauliflower for the topping), a dish I'd happily cook. I've since taught the code to pick "rescue" dishes like cottage pie (almost any root veg or cauliflower makes the topping), but a bigger model would know far more dishes like it on its own. The model is one setting, so the same app can run larger open-weight models such as gpt-oss-20b (OpenAI's open-weight model), Gemma 3 27B or Qwen 3. They write better recipes and follow the rules more reliably, and need less checking in code. On a machine with 16 GB+ of RAM that's just MODEL=gpt-oss:20b python3 app.py. For a paid version, the same open models could run on a hosted server, while keeping the free, private local mode as the default.
  • A phone app. Shoppers need it in the shop, not at their laptop. Small Gemma models already run on phones, so an on-device version would work offline in the supermarket aisle, with nobody's shopping data leaving the phone.
  • Snap the fridge. gemma3 can read images, so the next step is uploading a photo of the fridge and letting it list the ingredients for you.
  • A shopping list built from "You'd also need" across the week.
  • Café mode extras: pricing suggestions, allergen labels, and a printable specials board.
  • Fine-tuning on a café's own menu, so the specials match its style.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For this project, open made it practical:

  • It costs nothing to run. Every request runs on my laptop. A café could generate specials all day and never see a bill. With a paid API, cost per request would decide whether this works as a business at all.
  • The savings stay with the people who need them. An app that helps a tight budget shouldn't come with a subscription. Running an open model locally means every dollar saved on food stays saved.
  • It's private. What's in your fridge, what you eat and your diet never leave your computer. For a café, its stock levels and supplier details stay in-house.
  • It works offline. No internet, no problem. It also keeps working if a provider changes its prices or shuts down a model.
  • It's swappable. One environment variable (MODEL=llama3.2 python3 app.py) switches to a different open model. Nobody can lock me in.

My First User

My sister and a friend. My sister sent me what was in her fridge, and a friend sent me a photo of hers. I typed both into Fridge2Fork and sent back the recipes. Their suggestion back was the best feedback I got all week: "Wouldn't this be great at the grocery store?" Supermarkets mark food down when it has to be eaten that day. Someone on a tight budget could type in the specials, see what they could make, and decide what to buy. That became 🛒 On a budget mode.

And honestly, me. This answered my own "what should we have for dinner?" problem, which is exactly why I built it. It suggested an asparagus and sweet potato soup. I cooked it in my soup maker, turned the leftover carrots and half a sweet potato into roasted veg chips, and toasted two slices of bread from the freezer for dipping. Nothing in that dinner was bought for it.

A market seller. I told a fresh produce seller at my local market about the app. He said it would be great to see, because so much of his produce doesn't meet "quality" standards and has to be thrown away. That's where the "rescue box + recipe card" idea came from.

Did anyone pay? Not yet: it's a week old and runs on my laptop. But the market seller is the clearest lead. His imperfect produce is money he currently throws away, and a recipe card that helps it sell is something a small business could pay for.

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma. gemma3 (4B) is the whole engine of Fridge2Fork. It runs locally on a laptop CPU through Ollama (7 GB RAM, no GPU) and writes every recipe from what's actually in your fridge, spice rack and cupboard.

What I learned about using it well:

  • Strict JSON output (format: "json") with a fixed set of fields lets recipes drop straight into the page, with validation and retries for the odd broken reply.
  • Tight constraints help a small model. "Season only with the spices listed" turned generic recipes into ones I could actually cook.
  • Check the important rules in code. The model mostly follows instructions, so a small server-side filter removes anything from "also need" that the user already has.
  • A small context (2,560 tokens) keeps it inside a 7 GB laptop's memory, and short prompts and replies keep it fast: one idea at a time, in about a minute.

It shows that a 4B open model on an ordinary laptop is good enough to plan dinner, for free.

Best Use of ElevenLabs. I used ElevenLabs to generate the narration for my demo. Fridge2Fork runs on a laptop with 7 GB of RAM, and when I tried to record myself talking while gemma3 was running, the laptop ran out of memory and crashed. So I recorded the app silently, wrote a script, and had an ElevenLabs voice read it over the top. The opening image of the fridge was made with ElevenLabs Image too.

That fits the app's idea. The heavy work runs locally, and the voice is added afterwards, so nothing about your fridge leaves the laptop. Next, I'd like Fridge2Fork to read the steps out loud while you cook, so you don't have to touch the screen with floury hands.

title: EIA's January "forecast" of this year's solar additions was the developers' plan, 2020-2024
summary:
Every January EIA publishes two numbers for how much utility-scale solar will be added that year. Today in Energy reports what developers plan, from the EIA-860M inventory. The Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO), the same month, says what EIA forecasts. Last week I compared the two for 2025 and called it one year, not a track record. So I pulled the archived STEO PDFs for 2020-2025, wrote four predictions down before reading the 2020-2022 editions, and scored both numbers against what EIA's own Form EIA-860 finally recorded.

For solar in 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2024 the two numbers were the same number. The STEO's own capacity table implies same-year solar additions of 13.5, 15.4, 21.4 and 36.4 GW. The developers' plans were 13.5, 15.4, 21.5 and 36.4 GW. Wind agreed within 0.3 GW in 2020-2023. The STEO carried the EIA-860M schedule into its forecast rather than discounting it.

What the scoring shows:

  • Neither was better. Over 12 solar and wind cases, 2020-2025, the STEO was closer to the final in 5, the plan in 6, with one tie. Mean solar error: STEO 6.0 GW, plan 5.7 GW.
  • Both overshot solar almost every year. The plan was above the final in all six years, the STEO in five. In 2022 both were about 10 GW too high (21 GW expected, 11.1 GW built).
  • EIA departed from the schedule three times. 2024 wind: STEO 7.0 GW against 8.2 planned, 5.2 built, so the discount helped. 2025 solar: 25.7 against 32.5, 29.5 built, so it over-corrected and 2025 is the only year the STEO was under the final. 2023 solar: the STEO was above the plan (31.7 against 29.1; 18.9 built).
  • All four pre-registered predictions held, and the result is stronger than I predicted: I expected the STEO to sit within 3 GW of the plan, not to match it to 0.1 GW.
  • Stated in advance for 2026: the January 2026 STEO's solar figure is within 2 GW of the 43.4 GW plan, and the 2026 final comes in below both. Scored when the data arrive.

EIA does not hide this. The January 2023 edition says "Power generators plan to add 32 GW", and the article on the January 2021 edition says "Power developers are scheduled to add 15.4 GW". But I found no place where the two series had been put side by side against what was built, and when the press reports "EIA forecasts N GW of solar this year", it is until 2025 reporting the developers' schedule.

Every figure was read twice (the narrative sentence and the capacity table), the sentence extractor, the CSV, the pre-registration and the limits (net change versus gross additions, sector, rounding) are in the repository: https://github.com/munimtechnologies/eia860m-slip/blob/main/docs/steo-vs-plan.md

I am MV2 of Munim, Inc. The code, data compilation and this post were made with AI agents working in my name.

title: Menu-Sahayak: Instant Allergen Insights for Indian Restaurant Menus (Powered by Llama 3.3)
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

Menu-Sahayak is a lightweight web app that analyzes Indian restaurant menus and flags likely allergens per dish.

Tourists with food allergies often struggle to read Hindi or regional-language menus. Generic translation tools will tell you what "Chole Bhature" means, but they won't tell you it contains gluten and dairy. Menu-Sahayak bridges that gap. Paste a menu, and instantly get dish names alongside clear allergen tags (dairy, nuts, gluten, eggs, soy) and a practical safety note for each item.

It solves a very real, high-stakes problem for travelers and locals alike, making dining out safer and stress-free.

Demo

Here is a quick look at the interface:
(Apna screenshot yahan upload karein — DEV editor mein image icon par click karke)

Code

uxzwal / Menu-Sahayak

Allergen Lens — Menu Allergen Checker for Indian Restaurants

A lightweight Gradio app that analyzes Indian restaurant menu items and flags likely allergens per dish.

Powered by Llama 3.3 70B (open-weight) via Groq.

What it does

Paste menu items (one dish per line), and the app returns a numbered list with:

  • dish name
  • likely allergens from: dairy, nuts, gluten, eggs, soy
  • one concise safety note

The model is instructed to avoid unsupported certainty: allergens are marked as likely/possible based on common preparation, and users should verify with restaurant staff for severe allergies.

Why this is useful

Tourists with allergies may struggle to read Hindi or regional-language menus. This tool provides quick, practical allergen guidance dish-by-dish.

Setup

  1. Clone this repository.
  2. Install dependencies: 
    pip install -r menu-sahayak/requirements.txt
  3. Create env file: 
    cp menu-sahayak/.env.example menu-sahayak/.env
  4. Add your Groq API key in menu-sahayak/.env: 
    GROQ_API_KEY=your_key_here
  5. Run: 
    cd menu-sahayak
python app.py

Get a free Groq…

View on GitHub

How I Built It

  • Model: Llama 3.3 70B (open-weight) served via Groq's fast inference API.
  • Frontend/UI: Python + Gradio (customized theme for a clean, mobile-friendly dashboard feel).
  • The Core Logic: The app streams the response from the model and uses a highly specific system prompt to force the model into an "Allergen Analyst" persona. Instead of creative writing, it outputs structured, numbered allergen lists.
  • Error Handling: Built-in graceful fallbacks for missing API keys, rate limits, and empty inputs.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

I chose Llama 3.3 70B (open-weight) over a closed API because:

  1. Cost-Effective for a Side Hustle: Groq's generous free tier makes this app ₹0 to run. A closed model with similar reasoning capabilities would charge per token, eating into the thin margins of a side project.
  2. Model Swap Freedom: Because the logic is built around an open-weight model, I am not locked into one provider. If I want to swap Llama for Qwen or Gemma tomorrow to improve allergy detection, it's a one-line change.
  3. Transparency and Control: Open weights mean I know exactly what is processing the user's input. For an app dealing with health and dietary safety, this transparency is crucial.

The open pieces aren't just a buzzword here — the entire product is built around an accessible, open-weight model that I can control, prompt, and eventually self-host if needed.

title: Product Autopsy: My Auditor Flagged 18 Broken Promises in My Own Repos. Four Were Real
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

My own README told readers: “Push it before publishing this table, or remove the row until it is.”

That sentence is a note to the author. It had been sitting in a public repository for about two months, visible to everyone who opened it, and I hadn’t noticed. A tool I wrote found it.

The tool is Product Autopsy. A seller can have a polished listing and still ship a product that breaks its promises: “includes setup.xlsx”, “totals update automatically”, “ready in five minutes”. Most AI tools for sellers help write the listing. Product Autopsy checks the listing against the actual files, using deterministic checks where possible and a local model when the wording is too varied to parse. It reads a product folder the way a disappointed buyer would:

  • Missing files. The docs mention a file that isn’t in the package.
  • Broken links. A local link doesn’t resolve: a missing target, the wrong letter case, a path that escapes the package, or a #anchor with no matching heading.
  • Wrong spreadsheet totals. A SUM range that doesn’t match its data, a total that sums the wrong column, or a result that differs from the number the README promises. A small local model proposes claims from the prose. Plain code decides what is true. A validator rejects claims that fail the source-grounding and workbook checks, leaving them for human review rather than silently repairing them.

I ran it on 30 of my own public repositories. It flagged 18 candidates. I opened every one by hand: 4 were real, all from one repository, and I fixed them in one commit. The other 14 were false alarms, and they taught me more than the hits did.

Who would pay for this

Anyone who sells a digital download and gets support emails that start with “the file you mentioned isn’t in the zip”: spreadsheet and template sellers, authors of guides with companion files, people shipping starter kits. A broken promise costs a refund, a bad review or a support thread. And the thing being audited is usually a product that hasn’t been released yet, which is why it matters that this runs on the seller’s own laptop.

My hypothesis for the business: keep the audit free and local, and charge for a written report, batch audits of a whole catalogue, or a hosted version. That is a hypothesis. Nobody has paid for this, and the “My First User” section says exactly what I did and didn’t test.

Demo

FAIL  spreadsheet   tracker.xlsx: `Total Revenue`: the SUM range does not match the data rows; the result differs from the number the README promises

A clean control. All 3 checks pass for this product:

$ python autopsy.py samples_phrasing/tutor-tracker-right --report
Product Autopsy report: tutor-tracker-right
0 problem(s) found, 3 check(s) passed

No problems found among the promises this version can check.

Flagged path What it turned out to be
run_experiment2.py A leftover author note in the README, “Push it before publishing this table”, about a table row that no longer existed

In graph-density-engine the only remaining row is results.json, a file a command creates when it runs. The repo has the checker, the benchmark and hold-out generators, the Gemma claim extractor and the scripts that produce every table in this post.

Run it

You need Python, Git and Ollama installed. Install the Python dependency and download the model once:

pip install openpyxl
ollama pull gemma3:1b

Make sure Ollama is running before starting the model experiments. Then run:

python run_all.py gemma3:1b --real

run_all.py generates the benchmark, runs the checks, clones my 30 repositories if they are not already present, scans them, runs both hold-out experiments and saves the results to results.md. python autopsy.py samples/budget-planner --report

The synthetic benchmarks and hold-out experiments are generated by these commands. The prompt-v1 results came from an earlier prompt version and are saved in results_1b_prompt_v1.md. The original scan of my repositories was run before the fixes; the command reuses existing repository folders and does not recreate that pre-fix state. The saved outputs include results_before_fix.md, real_findings_before_fix.csv, real_findings_after_fix.csv and my manual verdicts in verify_findings.md. The first realistic-README run, which caught 5 of 10 wrong totals, is saved in results_noisy_run1.txt.

How I Built It

The stack is deliberately small: Python’s standard library, openpyxl to read .xlsx files, and Gemma 3 1B running locally through Ollama. No API keys and no calls to outside services during a check; the model runs on the same machine.

The model reads, the code judges

The three checks themselves (missing files, broken links and spreadsheet totals) use no model. The model is there because promises come in endless wordings. A regex handles the one phrasing I wrote it for, while a model can read “revenue comes to 1,640 in total” and “the sample revenue column sums to 1,640” as the same kind of claim. The model has one job: read the prose and return claims such as “the Total Revenue cell shows 1,640”, as JSON, with the schema enforced and the temperature at 0. It never decides whether a claim is true. Every claim must pass five checks in plain code, or it goes to human review and is never repaired:

  1. It matches the expected JSON structure and uses a supported claim type.
  2. It comes from a file that exists in the product.
  3. The claim text appears in that file (ignoring case, spacing and Markdown marks).
  4. The promised number appears inside that claim text.
  5. The target is one of the total labels that code read from the workbook itself, and its key word appears in the claim text. That last rule came out of a failure, described below.

Benchmark one: 30 planted defects

I generated 10 sample products with a script. Each has one planted defect per category (missing file, broken link, wrong spreadsheet total) plus valid controls, 60 valid checks in all, so false alarms can be measured. The ground truth lives in a separate file the checker never sees.

Category Planted defects Recall Precision False-positive rate
Missing file 10 100% 100% 0%
Broken link 10 100% 100% 0%
Spreadsheet 10 80% 100% 0%
All 30 93% 100% 0%

The two misses are on purpose. In two products I wrote the promised total in free phrasing (“revenue comes to 1,640 in total”) that my regex can’t parse. That gap is where a model should help.

I wrote both the generator and the checker, so these numbers show the engine works. They don’t show it finds defects in the wild. The next two sections are the ones that matter.

Benchmark two: what Gemma 1B actually did

I ran it on a CPU-only laptop with 7.4 GiB of RAM, about 1.1 GiB of it free, and no usable GPU. It took three experiments, because the first one gave an answer I didn’t trust.

Experiment 1: the main benchmark. Two of the products promise a total in free phrasing that my regex can’t parse. I tried two prompts.

Run Claims accepted Rejected by the validator New defects caught Spurious findings
Deterministic only n/a n/a n/a 0
Gemma 1B, prompt v1 7 23 0 0
Gemma 1B, prompt v2 (workbook labels and one worked example) 5 2 0 0

Prompt v1 produced mostly noise: 23 of 30 claims were rejected. For v2, my code read the real total labels from each workbook and handed them to the model along with one example from a different domain. Rejections fell to 2, but recall did not move. All 5 accepted claims were the same sentence my regex already handled, and the model never extracted either free-phrased promise.

The two rejected claims show why the validator exists. For one product, the model quoted “Etsy Profit Sheet helps you see profit per listing. Everything lives in one workbook.” and attached the number 1537. For another it quoted “Import categories.csv into the Categories tab.” and attached 1475. Neither number appears in either sentence. Without the grounding rule, those values would have been compared against real workbook totals and could have produced false accusations against a seller.

That looked like a clear answer, but it rested on two products, and I had adjusted the prompt after seeing them. So I built a fresh test.

Experiments 2 and 3: a hold-out set. I generated 20 new products. Each has a correct workbook and one sentence promising the Total Revenue in natural wording. There are 10 different phrasings, each used twice: once with the wrong number (a defect) and once with the right number (a control). None of the sentences matches my regex, so the deterministic baseline catches 0 of 10. I did not change the prompt after seeing these results. I ran the same 20 products twice: once with a one-sentence README, and once with a realistic README around the promise (a file list, setup steps, links, and an unrelated sentence saying “every total updates automatically”).

Setting Deterministic baseline Gemma 1B False alarms
Main benchmark: 2 free-phrased promises in realistic READMEs 0 of 2 0 of 2 0
Hold-out, one sentence per README 0 of 10 8 of 10 0 of 10 controls
Hold-out, realistic README around the promise, run 1 0 of 10 5 of 10 0 of 10 controls
Hold-out, realistic README around the promise, run 2 0 of 10 4 of 10 0 of 10 controls

Gemma 1B does add recall: it catches wrong totals that my deterministic checks can’t read. It is also fragile. Wrapping the same sentences in a realistic README cost 30 to 40 points of recall. In the noisy run the validator rejected 6 claims: 4 were spreadsheet claims with no number and 2 quoted text that couldn’t be found in the README. In all three hold-out runs none of the 10 correct promises was flagged, so no false accusation came out of these tests, though 10 controls per setting is a small check.

Three cautions. First, the realistic-README result isn’t stable: I ran it twice with the same code, the same data and the temperature at 0, and the results were not identical: 5 of 10, then 4 of 10 (repair-desk-wrong was caught once and missed once). The one-sentence set and the main benchmark reproduced exactly. Second, ten defects per setting is a small sample, so I wouldn’t call 80% against 40–50% a solid difference; I’d call it a warning. Third, I built both the products and the phrasings, so these results are still synthetic. They show where a small model starts to fail, not how it performs on real listings. I haven’t tested a larger Gemma, and I haven’t compared against a hosted model, so I won’t claim anything about either.

The real test: 30 of my own repos

I cloned and scanned 30 of my public repositories. The scan covered 216 checks: 206 file mentions and 10 local links. All 10 local links resolved. The file-mention check flagged 18 candidates, which I then reviewed manually.

I classified each flag as a confirmed defect, an expected absence, or uncertain, by opening the file and reading the surrounding text.

Verdict Count Why
Confirmed defect 4 One leftover note, two missing data files, one stale comment
Expected absence 14 Example paths in a sample agent chat, an archived design table and a simulated repo (9); a file a command creates when it runs (1); a negation, “No requirements.txt” (1); an example argument (1); a path on the reader’s own machine (1); an identifier in prose (1)

The four real rows come from three causes, all in graph-density-engine:

  • A leftover note to the author in the README, “Push it before publishing this table”, about a table row that no longer existed.
  • Missing data files. During the original scan, the README's Quick Start loaded incident_01 through DatasetLoader, but the required dataset JSON files were absent. On a fresh clone at that time, the Quick Start failed with FileNotFoundError. I reproduced it before restoring the files. I regenerated the datasets with fixed seeds, but I cannot prove they are byte-identical to the originals used for the published experiment.
  • A stale comment in requirements.txt pointing to agents/llm.py, a file that doesn’t exist, while the README says there is no model anywhere in the pipeline. The fix is one commit: c93d44e. I couldn’t find my original data files, so I regenerated them with the generator’s fixed seeds. The generator uses a fixed seed for each scenario, so the files should match, but I can’t prove they are byte-identical to the ones behind my published numbers, and I’d rather say so than imply it.

After the fix, a rescan flags 14, and every one is a false alarm I had already classified. Zero confirmed defects remain, which shows the find-and-fix loop works. It doesn’t show the repos are clean. The scan outputs from before and after the fix are saved in the repo, so the 18-to-14 change can be checked.

Precision on real repositories was 4 of 18, about 22%, and all four came from a single repo. I’d call the file-mention check useful for finding candidates and not yet good enough to trust unattended. Before scanning my own repos I tuned the noise filters on four third-party template repos, so those four don’t count as a clean test. The only change I made after seeing my own results was the path fix described below.

Two bugs the checker had

Running on real machines found two bugs in my own tool.

  • Windows hid case-mismatch links. On my Windows laptop, broken-link recall was 80% and overall recall was 87%, lower than on Linux. My code used Path.resolve(), which on Windows rewrites a path to its real on-disk case, so Guide.MD pointing at guide.md looked fine. It would break for a Linux reader. I replaced it with plain path arithmetic, and the numbers matched on both systems.
  • Paths that climb a folder. A mention of ../RESOLVER_RULES.md was flagged as missing even though the file exists. I fixed the path handling. This is a correctness fix made after seeing the real-repo results, and I’m reporting it as one.

What it can’t see

  • It skips fenced code blocks to avoid noise from examples, so a file listed in a README’s code-fenced tree can slip through. My graph-density-engine README lists phase2_results.json in its project tree, and that file isn’t in the repo. The checker missed it.
  • It reads files and never runs a product’s instructions. A Quick Start that fails when you run it is invisible to a tool that only reads. Running the instructions, the “buyer disappointment simulator” in my original pitch, is the obvious next build.
  • I have no recall number for real repos. I know what it flagged. I don’t know what it missed.

What I’d build next

  1. Test a larger Gemma on the realistic-README hold-out set, where the 1B model drops to 40–50%.
  2. Flag a file mention only when it sits in an instruction like “open”, “copy” or “run”, to cut the false alarms, and test that on a fresh set of repos.
  3. Run the Quick Start itself.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • The product folder never leaves the machine. The thing being audited is often unreleased work. Sending a seller’s unpublished files to a hosted API is a poor trade for a pre-launch check, and with a local model it isn’t needed.
  • The model is replaceable. The checker doesn’t care which model fills the claim slot. Swapping Gemma 1B for a larger local model means changing one tag, and I can measure the difference with the same benchmark.
  • No per-audit API fee. The audit runs locally with Python, openpyxl and a downloaded Gemma model. There is no hosted-model charge per check, although the model still needs storage, hardware and electricity. That is what makes a free local tier possible at all.
  • The design doesn’t depend on trusting the model. The validator is designed to reject unsupported claims before they become findings. That reduces one class of model error, but it doesn’t guarantee that every accepted finding is correct. In my runs, a 1B model caught up to 80% of the wrong totals my regex couldn’t read, fell to between 40% and 50% with realistic text around the promise, and produced no false alarms on the controls, though the tests are small. Where open fell short: the 1B model is fragile. Recall dropped from 80% to between 40% and 50% when I added realistic text around the promise, and a larger local model might fix that, which I haven’t tested. I haven’t compared against a hosted model, so I can’t tell you whether a closed API would have done better. What I can say is that an open model made the privacy and cost story possible, and the validator provided a checkable boundary around what the model could submit as a finding.

My First User

My first and only user so far is me, on 30 repos. No seller has tried it, and nobody has paid. I won’t claim that anyone would, because I don’t know.

What I do know is that it surfaced four things I had missed in my own published work, and that the false alarms are as informative as the hits: they show exactly where a seller would get annoyed. The next test that matters is handing it to a seller and asking whether the flags helped or irritated them.

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma

Gemma 3 1B, run locally through Ollama on a CPU-only laptop, reads README prose that my regex can't parse and proposes claims as JSON. On a hold-out of 20 products it caught 8 of 10 wrong totals in short READMEs (baseline: 0) and 4 or 5 of 10 in realistic ones. Most of this post is about what it took to make a 1B model's claims safe to act on: a validator that rejects anything it can't ground in the source. The tables are in "How I Built It".

Everything lives in one workbook.” and attached the number 1537. For another it quoted “Import categories.csv into the Categories tab.” and attached 1475. Neither number appears in either sentence. Without the grounding rule, those values would have been compared against real workbook totals and could have produced false accusations against a seller.

That looked like a clear answer, but it rested on two products, and I had adjusted the prompt after seeing them. So I built a fresh test.

Experiments 2 and 3: a hold-out set. I generated 20 new products. Each has a correct workbook and one sentence promising the Total Revenue in natural wording. There are 10 different phrasings, each used twice: once with the wrong number (a defect) and once with the right number (a control). None of the sentences matches my regex, so the deterministic baseline catches 0 of 10. I did not change the prompt after seeing these results. I ran the same 20 products twice: once with a one-sentence README, and once with a realistic README around the promise (a file list, setup steps, links, and an unrelated sentence saying “every total updates automatically”).

Gemma 1B does add recall: it catches wrong totals that my deterministic checks can’t read. It is also fragile. Wrapping the same sentences in a realistic README cost 30 to 40 points of recall. In the noisy run the validator rejected 6 claims: 4 were spreadsheet claims with no number and 2 quoted text that couldn’t be found in the README. In all three hold-out runs none of the 10 correct promises was flagged, so no false accusation came out of these tests, though 10 controls per setting is a small check.

Three cautions. First, the realistic-README result isn’t stable: I ran it twice with the same code, the same data and the temperature at 0, and the results were not identical: 5 of 10, then 4 of 10 (repair-desk-wrong was caught once and missed once). The one-sentence set and the main benchmark reproduced exactly. Second, ten defects per setting is a small sample, so I wouldn’t call 80% against 40–50% a solid difference; I’d call it a warning. Third, I built both the products and the phrasings, so these results are still synthetic. They show where a small model starts to fail, not how it performs on real listings. I haven’t tested a larger Gemma, and I haven’t compared against a hosted model, so I won’t claim anything about either.

The real test: 30 of my own repos

I cloned and scanned 30 of my public repositories. The scan covered 216 checks: 206 file mentions and 10 local links. All 10 local links resolved. The file-mention check flagged 18 candidates, which I then reviewed manually.

I classified each flag as a confirmed defect, an expected absence, or uncertain, by opening the file and reading the surrounding text.

Verdict Count Why
Confirmed defect 4 One leftover note, two missing data files, one stale comment
Expected absence 14 Example paths in a sample agent chat, an archived design table and a simulated repo (9); a file a command creates when it runs (1); a negation, “No requirements.txt” (1); an example argument (1); a path on the reader’s own machine (1); an identifier in prose (1)

The four real rows come from three causes, all in graph-density-engine:

  • A leftover note to the author in the README, “Push it before publishing this table”, about a table row that no longer existed.
  • Missing data files. During the original scan, the README's Quick Start loaded incident_01 through DatasetLoader, but the required dataset JSON files were absent. On a fresh clone at that time, the Quick Start failed with FileNotFoundError. I reproduced it before restoring the files. I regenerated the datasets with fixed seeds, but I cannot prove they are byte-identical to the originals used for the published experiment.
  • A stale comment in requirements.txt pointing to agents/llm.py, a file that doesn’t exist, while the README says there is no model anywhere in the pipeline. The fix is one commit: c93d44e. I couldn’t find my original data files, so I regenerated them with the generator’s fixed seeds. The generator uses a fixed seed for each scenario, so the files should match, but I can’t prove they are byte-identical to the ones behind my published numbers, and I’d rather say so than imply it.

After the fix, a rescan flags 14, and every one is a false alarm I had already classified. Zero confirmed defects remain, which shows the find-and-fix loop works. It doesn’t show the repos are clean. The scan outputs from before and after the fix are saved in the repo, so the 18-to-14 change can be checked.

Precision on real repositories was 4 of 18, about 22%, and all four came from a single repo. I’d call the file-mention check useful for finding candidates and not yet good enough to trust unattended. Before scanning my own repos I tuned the noise filters on four third-party template repos, so those four don’t count as a clean test. The only change I made after seeing my own results was the path fix described below.

Two bugs the checker had

Running on real machines found two bugs in my own tool.

  • Windows hid case-mismatch links. On my Windows laptop, broken-link recall was 80% and overall recall was 87%, lower than on Linux. My code used Path.resolve(), which on Windows rewrites a path to its real on-disk case, so Guide.MD pointing at guide.md looked fine. It would break for a Linux reader. I replaced it with plain path arithmetic, and the numbers matched on both systems.
  • Paths that climb a folder. A mention of ../RESOLVER_RULES.md was flagged as missing even though the file exists. I fixed the path handling. This is a correctness fix made after seeing the real-repo results, and I’m reporting it as one.

What it can’t see

  • It skips fenced code blocks to avoid noise from examples, so a file listed in a README’s code-fenced tree can slip through. My graph-density-engine README lists phase2_results.json in its project tree, and that file isn’t in the repo. The checker missed it.
  • It reads files and never runs a product’s instructions. A Quick Start that fails when you run it is invisible to a tool that only reads. Running the instructions, the “buyer disappointment simulator” in my original pitch, is the obvious next build.
  • I have no recall number for real repos. I know what it flagged. I don’t know what it missed.

What I’d build next

  1. Test a larger Gemma on the realistic-README hold-out set, where the 1B model drops to 40–50%.
  2. Flag a file mention only when it sits in an instruction like “open”, “copy” or “run”, to cut the false alarms, and test that on a fresh set of repos.
  3. Run the Quick Start itself.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • The product folder never leaves the machine. The thing being audited is often unreleased work. Sending a seller’s unpublished files to a hosted API is a poor trade for a pre-launch check, and with a local model it isn’t needed.
  • The model is replaceable. The checker doesn’t care which model fills the claim slot. Swapping Gemma 1B for a larger local model means changing one tag, and I can measure the difference with the same benchmark.
  • No per-audit API fee. The audit runs locally with Python, openpyxl and a downloaded Gemma model. There is no hosted-model charge per check, although the model still needs storage, hardware and electricity. That is what makes a free local tier possible at all.
  • The design doesn’t depend on trusting the model. The validator is designed to reject unsupported claims before they become findings. That reduces one class of model error, but it doesn’t guarantee that every accepted finding is correct. In my runs, a 1B model caught up to 80% of the wrong totals my regex couldn’t read, fell to between 40% and 50% with realistic text around the promise, and produced no false alarms on the controls, though the tests are small. Where open fell short: the 1B model is fragile. Recall dropped from 80% to between 40% and 50% when I added realistic text around the promise, and a larger local model might fix that, which I haven’t tested. I haven’t compared against a hosted model, so I can’t tell you whether a closed API would have done better. What I can say is that an open model made the privacy and cost story possible, and the validator provided a checkable boundary around what the model could submit as a finding.

My First User

My first and only user so far is me, on 30 repos. No seller has tried it, and nobody has paid. I won’t claim that anyone would, because I don’t know.

What I do know is that it surfaced four things I had missed in my own published work, and that the false alarms are as informative as the hits: they show exactly where a seller would get annoyed. The next test that matters is handing it to a seller and asking whether the flags helped or irritated them.
